title: Embedding quantization and rescoring
summary: Store each vector component in fewer bits (int8 or one bit), search the compressed index for extra candidates, then rescore them with the original vectors. You get a large memory saving with a small recall cost.
useIf: Vector memory is the cost driver and you can afford a rescoring step against original vectors.
avoidIf: The index is small or dimensions are low. Binary quantization on small vectors loses too much.

explain.md: **Quantization** shrinks vectors. **Scalar quantization** stores each float32 component as an 8-bit integer, about 4 times smaller. **Binary quantization** keeps one bit per dimension, up to about 28 to 32 times smaller. Compressed vectors are cheaper to hold in memory and faster to compare, but they are less precise, so the compressed search returns a rougher top list.

explain.title: Oversample, then rescore
explain.alt: The query searches the compressed index and returns k times the oversampling factor candidates. Those candidates are rescored with the original vectors and the top k are returned.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  Q["Query vector"] --> C["Search compressed index"]
  C --> O["k x oversampling candidates"]
  O --> R["Rescore with original vectors"]
  R --> T["Top k results"]

explain.md: **Oversampling and rescoring** recover the lost precision. With `defaultOversampling` of 4 and a query `k` of 50, the engine fetches 200 candidates from the compressed vectors, recomputes similarity with the originals and returns the best 50. In AI Search, rescoring works only with HNSW, and `rescoreStorageMethod` is `preserveOriginals` or `discardOriginals` (binary only). A quantized field needs a new vector profile and a new field. Binary quantization is best for dimensions above 1,024 and for embeddings centred on zero [[tr6]] [[tr10]].

items.label: Scalar (int8)
items.note: About 99.3% of float32 performance in an open benchmark [[tr23]]

items.label: Binary
items.note: AI Search says up to 28 times [[tr6]]. About 96% retained with rescoring, 92.5% without [[tr23]]

explain.title: Compression with rescoring (AI Search index definition)
explain.caption: Shape follows the Create Index documentation [[tr10]]. Attach the compression to a vector profile, then to a new vector field.

explain.md: Keeping originals (`preserveOriginals`) costs storage but keeps rescoring and later re-quantization possible. Discarding them (binary only) saves the most space and removes both. Always measure recall against an uncompressed baseline on your own queries before and after.

whereToUse: Indexes of tens or hundreds of millions of vectors where memory sets the service cost
Pipelines combined with Matryoshka truncation for the largest saving
Any HNSW index where a rescoring step with full vectors is acceptable

use: Memory or cost per vector is the bottleneck
Dimensions are high and embeddings are centred on zero (binary)
avoid: Small indexes where memory is not a constraint
Setups that cannot store or fetch original vectors for rescoring
flips: Recall falls short: increase oversampling or keep originals
Dimensions are modest: choose scalar quantization over binary
You need to change settings later: preserve originals

pitfalls.symptom: Recall drops badly after enabling binary quantization on 384-dimension vectors
pitfalls.cause: Binary quantization suits dimensions above 1,024 and zero-centred embeddings
pitfalls.fix: Use scalar quantization for low dimensions, or test binary with rescoring first

pitfalls.symptom: You cannot change the oversampling strategy or requantize later
pitfalls.fix: Use `preserveOriginals` until the settings are final and recall is proven

pitfalls.symptom: Enabling compression on an existing field is rejected
pitfalls.cause: A quantized field needs a new vector profile and a new field
pitfalls.fix: Add the new field and re-embed or copy vectors, then cut over by alias

pitfalls.symptom: Rescoring has no effect on a non-HNSW field
pitfalls.cause: In AI Search, rescoring works only with HNSW
pitfalls.fix: Use an HNSW algorithm in the vector profile

scenarios.title: 100 million high-dimension vectors
scenarios.situation: An index holds 100 million 3,072-dimension vectors and costs far more than planned. A labelled query set exists and a rescoring step is acceptable.
scenarios.question: Which compression do you test first?

options.name: Binary quantization with oversampling and rescoring, originals preserved
options.why: High dimensions are where binary works, and rescoring against originals recovers most of the quality.
options.tradeoff: A new field and some storage for originals.

options.name: Scalar int8 only
options.why: Safe and simple, about 4 times smaller.
options.tradeoff: Much less saving than binary at this scale.

options.name: Binary with `discardOriginals` straight away
options.why: Removes rescoring and any chance to revise settings before recall is proven.
options.tradeoff: Right once recall is validated and storage must shrink further.

flips.if: Recall with binary and rescoring misses the target
flips.then: Fall back to scalar quantization or raise oversampling.
Reassess, since binary prefers high dimensions.

scenarios.takeaway: At extreme scale, compress hard but prove recall before discarding originals.

scenarios.title: Mid-size index, strict recall
scenarios.situation: An index of 5 million 1,536-dimension vectors fits the quota but the team wants headroom. Recall must stay within half a point of today.
unknowns: Can a new field be backfilled?
scenarios.question: What do you pick?

options.name: Scalar int8 with rescoring and originals preserved
options.why: A 4 times saving with about 99% of float32 performance in an open benchmark, and low tuning effort.
options.tradeoff: Originals still need storage and a new field must be filled.

options.name: Binary quantization with rescoring
options.why: A bigger saving that may still meet the target.
options.tradeoff: More recall risk and tuning than scalar.

options.name: Do nothing
options.why: Leaves the team with no headroom as the corpus grows.
options.tradeoff: Right while the index is far from its quota and growth is flat.

flips.then: Move to binary or add truncation.

scenarios.takeaway: Pick the lightest compression that meets the memory goal.

quiz.q: 100 million vectors of 1,024 dimensions are stored with binary quantization (1 bit per dimension). How large are the compressed vectors, in GB (1 GB = 10^9 bytes)?
quiz.explain: 1,024 bits = 128 bytes. 128 bytes x 100,000,000 = 12.8 billion bytes = 12.8 GB. Float32 would need 409.6 GB, so the ratio is 32.

quiz.q: Recall fell sharply after binary quantization on 384-dimension embeddings. What is the best next step?
options: Use scalar quantization or test binary with rescoring
quiz.explain: Binary quantization suits high dimensions (above 1,024), so low-dimension vectors should use scalar quantization, or binary with rescoring. Lowering efSearch and discarding originals reduce quality further, and overlap is a chunking dial.

quiz.q: Which statements about AI Search quantization are correct?
options: A quantized field can be enabled in place on an existing field
`discardOriginals` is available for binary quantization only
quiz.explain: The default oversampling is 4, rescoring needs HNSW and `discardOriginals` is binary only. A quantized field needs a new vector profile and a new field, not an in-place change.

flashcards.front: What does oversampling do in vector search with rescoring?
flashcards.back: It fetches k times a multiplier of candidates from the compressed index, rescoring them with original vectors before returning the top k. AI Search default: 4.

flashcards.front: How much do int8 and binary quantization save, and how much quality do they keep?
flashcards.back: int8: 4 times smaller, about 99.3% performance. Binary: 32 times smaller (AI Search says up to 28), about 96% with rescoring and 92.5% without.

flashcards.front: When is binary quantization a poor fit?
flashcards.back: For low-dimension vectors (below about 1,024) or embeddings not centred on zero. Use scalar quantization there.
